entries.e7a1a2a0ddd6bac0a2d1ea6d151aa28050be2a84: <div sID="gen31472" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="2Cor.4" sID="2Cor.4"/> <div eID="gen31472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31473" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31474" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have an account, I. Of the constancy of the apostle and his fellow-labourers in their work. Their constancy in declared (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">ver. 1</reference>), their sincerity is vouched (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">ver. 2</reference>), an objection is obviated (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3-2Cor.4.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>), and their integrity proved, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5-2Cor.4.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. II. Of their courage and patience under their sufferings. Where see what their sufferings were, together with their allays (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.12">ver. 8-12</reference>), and what it was that kept them from sinking and fainting under them, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13-2Cor.4.18">ver. 13, to the end</reference>.
entries.322283163ffb377eb1a4d4f0dba11f4e7d9825fe: <div eID="gen31474" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31473" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Constancy and Sincerity of the Apostles; The Apostle's Integrity. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31475" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not; <hi type="super">2</hi> But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: <hi type="super">4</hi> In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them. 5 For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake. <hi type="super">6</hi> For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to <hi type="italic">give</hi> the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. <hi type="super">7</hi> But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. <div eID="gen31475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31476" type="x-p"/> The apostle had, in the foregoing chapter, been <hi type="italic">magnifying his office,</hi> upon the consideration of the excellency or glory of that gospel about which he did officiate; and now in this chapter his design is to vindicate their ministry from the accusation of false teachers, who charged them as deceitful workers, or endeavoured to prejudice the minds of the people against them on account of their sufferings. He tells them, therefore, how they believed, and how they showed their value for their office as ministers of the gospel. They were not puffed up with pride, but spurred on to great diligence: "<hi type="italic">Seeing we have this ministry,</hi> are so much distinguished and dignified, we do not take state upon ourselves, nor indulge in idleness, but are excited to the better performance of our duty." <div eID="gen31476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31477" type="x-p"/> I. Two things in general we have an account of:—Their constancy and sincerity in their work and labour, concerning which observe, 1. Their constancy and perseverance in their work are declared: "<hi type="italic">We faint not</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">v. 1</reference>) under the difficulty of our work, nor do we desist from our labour." And this their stedfastness was owing to the <hi type="italic">mercy of God.</hi> From the same mercy and grace from which they received the apostleship (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.5">Rom. i. 5</reference>), they received strength to persevere in the work of that office. Note, As it is great mercy and grace to be called to be saints, and especially to be <hi type="italic">counted faithful, and be put into the ministry</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.12">1 Tim. i. 12</reference>), so it is owing to the mercy and grace of God if we continue faithful and persevere in our work with diligence. The best men in the world would faint in their work, and under their burdens, if they did not receive mercy from God. <hi type="italic">By the grace of God I am what I am,</hi> said this great apostle in his former epistle to these Corinthians, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.10">ch. xv. 10</reference>. And that mercy which has helped us out, and helped us on, hitherto, we may rely upon to help us even to the end. 2. Their sincerity in their work is avouched (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">v. 2</reference>) in several expressions: <hi type="italic">We have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty.</hi> The things of dishonesty are hidden things, that will not bear the light; and those who practise them are, or should be, ashamed of them, especially when they are known. Such things the apostle did not allow of, but did renounce and avoid with indignation: <hi type="italic">Not walking in craftiness,</hi> or in disguise, acting with art and cunning, but in great simplicity, and with open freedom. They had no base and wicked designs covered with fair and specious pretences of something that was good. Nor did they in their preaching <hi type="italic">handle the word of God deceitfully;</hi> but, as he said before, they used <hi type="italic">great plainness of speech,</hi> and did not make their ministry serve a turn, or truckle to base designs. They had not cheated the people with falsehood instead of truth. Some think the apostle alludes to the deceit which treacherous gamesters use, or that of hucksters in the market, who mix bad wares with good. The apostles acted not like such persons, but they <hi type="italic">manifested the truth to every man's conscience,</hi> declaring nothing but what in their own conscience they believed to be true, and what might serve for the conviction of their consciences who heard them, who were to judge for themselves, and to give an account for themselves. And all this they did <hi type="italic">as in the sight of God,</hi> desirous thus to commend themselves to God, and to the consciences of men, by their undisguised sincerity. Note, A stedfast adherence to the truths of the gospel will commend ministers and people; and sincerity or uprightness will preserve a man's reputation, and the good opinion of wise and good men concerning him. <div eID="gen31477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31478" type="x-p"/> II. An objection is obviated, which might be thus formed: "If it be thus, how then does it come to pass, that the gospel is hid, and proves ineffectual, as to some who hear it?" To which the apostle answers, by showing that this was not the fault of the gospel, nor of the preachers thereof. But the true reasons of this are, 1. <hi type="italic">Those are lost souls</hi> to whom the gospel is hid, or is ineffectual, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">v. 3</reference>. Christ came to <hi type="italic">save that which was lost</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">Matt. xvii. 11</reference>), and the gospel of Christ is sent to save such; and, if this do not find and save them, they are lost for ever; they must never expect any thing else to save them, for there is no other method or means of salvation. The hiding of the gospel therefore from souls is both an evidence and cause of their ruin. 2. <hi type="italic">The god of this world hath blinded their minds,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">v. 4</reference>. They are under the influence and power of the devil, who is here called <hi type="italic">the god of this world,</hi> and elsewhere <hi type="italic">the prince of this world,</hi> because of the great interest he has in this world, the homage that is paid to him by multitudes in this world, and the great sway that, by divine permission, he bears in the world, and in the hearts of his subjects, or rather slaves. And as he is the prince of darkness, and ruler of the darkness of this world, so he darkens the understandings of men, and increases their prejudices, and supports his interest by keeping them in the dark, blinding their minds with ignorance, and error, and prejudices, that they should not <hi type="italic">behold the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God.</hi> Observe, (1.) Christ's design by his gospel is to make a glorious discovery of God to the minds of men. Thus, as the image of God, he demonstrates the power and wisdom of God, and the grace and mercy of God for their salvation. But, (2.) The design of the devil is to keep men in ignorance; and, when he cannot keep the light of the gospel out of the world, he makes it his great business to keep it out of the hearts of men. <div eID="gen31478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31479" type="x-p"/> III. A proof of their integrity is given, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5">v. 5</reference>. They made it their business to preach Christ, and not themselves: <hi type="italic">We preach not ourselves.</hi> Self was not the matter nor the end of the apostles' preaching: they did not give their own notions and private opinions, nor their passions and prejudices, for the word and will of God; nor did they seek themselves, to advance their own secular interest or glory. But they <hi type="italic">preached Christ Jesus the Lord;</hi> and thus it did become them and behove them to do, as being Christ's servants. Their business was to make their Master known to the world as the Messiah, or the Christ of God, and as Jesus, the only Saviour of men, and as the rightful Lord, and to advance his honour and glory. Note, All the lines of Christian doctrine centre in Christ; and in preaching Christ we preach all we should preach. "As to <hi type="italic">ourselves,</hi>" says the apostle, "<hi type="italic">we preach,</hi> or declare, that <hi type="italic">we are your servants for Jesus' sake.</hi>" This was no compliment, but a real profession of a readiness to do good to their souls, and to promote their spiritual and eternal interest, and that for <hi type="italic">Jesus' sake;</hi> not for their own sake or their own advantage, but for Christ's sake, that they might imitate his great example, and advance his glory. Note, Ministers should not be of proud spirits, <hi type="italic">lording it over God's heritage,</hi> who are servants to the souls of men: yet, at the same time, they must avoid the meanness of spirit implied in becoming the servants of the humours or the lusts of men; if they should thus <hi type="italic">seek to please men, they would not be the servants of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Gal. i. 10</reference>. And there was good reason, 1. Why they should preach Christ. For by gospel light we have the <hi type="italic">knowledge of the glory of God,</hi> which shines in the <hi type="italic">face of Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">v. 6</reference>. And the light of this <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> is more glorious than that light which God commanded to shine out of darkness. It is a pleasant thing for the eye to behold the sun in the firmament; but it is more pleasant and profitable when the gospel shines in the heart. Note, As light was the first-born of the first creation, so it is in the new creation: the illumination of the Spirit is his first work upon the soul. The grace of God created such a light in the soul that those who <hi type="italic">were sometimes darkness are made light in the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>. 2. Why they should not preach themselves: because they were but earthen vessels, things of little or no worth or value. Here seems to be an allusion to the lamps which Gideon's soldiers carried in earthen pitchers, <reference osisRef="Judg.7.16">Jud. vii. 16</reference>. The treasure of gospel light and grace is put into earthen vessels. The ministers of the gospel are weak and frail creatures, and <hi type="italic">subject to like passions</hi> and infirmities as other men; they are mortal, and soon broken in pieces. And God has so ordered it that the weaker the vessels are the stronger his power may appear to be, that the treasure itself should be valued the more. Note, There is an excellency of power in the gospel of Christ, to enlighten the mind, to convince the conscience, to convert the soul, and to rejoice the heart; but all this power is from God the author, and not from men, who are but instruments, so that God in all things must be glorified.
entries.770dac6053038be57835296ea584d3f6b3f3768f: <div eID="gen31479" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Apostles' Sufferings and Supports. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 57.)</title> <div sID="gen31480" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">We are</hi> troubled on every side, yet not distressed; <hi type="italic">we are</hi> perplexed, but not in despair; <hi type="super">9</hi> Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed; <hi type="super">10</hi> Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body. 11 For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus' sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh. <hi type="super">12</hi> So then death worketh in us, but life in you. <hi type="super">13</hi> We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak; <hi type="super">14</hi> Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present <hi type="italic">us</hi> with you. <hi type="super">15</hi> For all things <hi type="italic">are</hi> for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God. <hi type="super">16</hi> For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward <hi type="italic">man</hi> is renewed day by day. <hi type="super">17</hi> For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding <hi type="italic">and</hi> eternal weight of glory; <hi type="super">18</hi> While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen <hi type="italic">are</hi> temporal; but the things which are not seen <hi type="italic">are</hi> eternal. <div eID="gen31480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31481" type="x-p"/> In these verses the apostle gives an account of their courage and patience under all their sufferings, where observe, <div eID="gen31481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31482" type="x-p"/> I. How their sufferings, and patience under them, are declared, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.12">v. 8-12</reference>. The apostles were great sufferers; therein they followed their Master: Christ had told them <hi type="italic">that in the world they should have tribulation,</hi> and so they had; yet they met with wonderful support, great relief, and many allays of their sorrows. "<hi type="italic">We are,</hi>" says the apostle, "<hi type="italic">troubled on every side,</hi> afflicted many ways, and we meet with almost all sorts of troubles; <hi type="italic">yet not distressed,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8">v. 8</reference>. We are not hedged in nor cooped up, because we can see help in God, and help from God, and have liberty of access to God." Again, "We are <hi type="italic">perplexed,</hi> often uncertain, and in doubt what will become of us, and not always without anxiety in our minds on this account; <hi type="italic">yet not in despair</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8">v. 8</reference>), even in our greatest perplexities, knowing that God is able to support us, and to deliver us, and in him we always place our trust and hope." Again, "We are <hi type="italic">persecuted</hi> by men, pursued with hatred and violence from place to place, as men not worthy to live; yet <hi type="italic">not forsaken</hi> of God," <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">v. 9</reference>. Good men may be sometimes forsaken of their friends, as well as persecuted by their enemies; but God will never leave them nor forsake them. Again, "We are sometimes dejected, or <hi type="italic">cast down;</hi> the enemy may in a great measure prevail, and our spirits begin to fail us; there may be fears within, as well as fightings without; yet we are <hi type="italic">not destroyed,</hi>" <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">v. 9</reference>. Still they were preserved, and kept their heads above water. Note, Whatever condition the children of God may be in, in this world, they have a "<hi type="italic">but not</hi>" to comfort themselves with; their case sometimes is bad, yea very bad, but not so bad as it might be. The apostle speaks of their sufferings as constant, and as a counterpart of the sufferings of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">v. 10</reference>. The sufferings of Christ were, after a sort, re-acted in the sufferings of Christians; thus did they <hi type="italic">bear about the dying of the Lord Jesus</hi> in their body, setting before the world the great example of a suffering Christ, <hi type="italic">that the life of Jesus might also be made manifest,</hi> that is, that people might see the power of Christ's resurrection, and the efficacy of grace in and from the living Jesus, manifested in and towards them, who did yet live, though they were always <hi type="italic">delivered to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">v. 11</reference>), and though <hi type="italic">death worked in them</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">v. 12</reference>), they being exposed to death, and ready to be swallowed up by death continually. So great were the sufferings of the apostles that, in comparison with them, other Christians were, even at this time, in prosperous circumstances: <hi type="italic">Death worketh in us; but life in you,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen31482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31483" type="x-p"/> II. What it was that kept them from sinking and fainting under their sufferings, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13-2Cor.4.18">v. 13-18</reference>. Whatever the burdens and troubles of good men may be, they have cause enough not to faint. <div eID="gen31483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31484" type="x-p"/> 1. Faith kept them from fainting: <hi type="italic">We have the same spirit of faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">v. 13</reference>), that faith which is of the operation of the Spirit; the same faith by which the saints of old did and suffered such great things. Note, The grace of faith is a sovereign cordial, and an effectual antidote against fainting-fits in troublous times. The spirit of faith will go far to bear up the spirit of a man under his infirmities; and as the apostle had David's example to imitate, who said (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Ps. cxvi. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have believed, and therefore have I spoken,</hi> so he leaves us his example to imitate: <hi type="italic">We also believe,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">and therefore speak.</hi> Note, As we receive help and encouragement from the good words and examples of others, so we should be careful to give a good example to others. <div eID="gen31484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31485" type="x-p"/> 2. Hope of the resurrection kept them from sinking, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.14">v. 14</reference>. They knew that Christ was raised, and that his resurrection was an earnest and assurance of theirs. This he had treated of largely in his former epistle to these Corinthians, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.1-1Cor.15.58">ch. xv</reference>. And therefore their hope was firm, being well grounded, that he who raised up Christ the head will also raise up all his members. Note, The hope of the resurrection will encourage us in a suffering day, and set us above the fear of death; for what reason has a good Christian to fear death, that dies in hope of a joyful resurrection? <div eID="gen31485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31486" type="x-p"/> 3. The consideration of the glory of God and the benefit of the church, by means of their sufferings, kept them from fainting, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">v. 15</reference>. Their sufferings were for the church's advantage (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.6">ch. i. 6</reference>), and thus did redound to God's glory. For, when the church is edified, then God is glorified; and we may well afford to bear sufferings patiently and cheerfully when we see others are the better for them—if they are instructed and edified, if they are confirmed and comforted. Note, The sufferings of Christ's ministers, as well as their preaching and conversation, are intended for the good of the church and the glory of God. <div eID="gen31486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31487" type="x-p"/> 4. The thoughts of the advantage their souls would reap by the sufferings of their bodies kept them from fainting: <hi type="italic">Though our outward man perish, our inward man is renewed day by day,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16">v. 16</reference>. Here note, (1.) We have every one of us an outward and an inward man, a body and a soul. (2.) If the outward man perish, there is no remedy, it must and will be so, it was made to perish. (3.) It is our happiness if the decays of the outward man do contribute to the renewing of the inward man, if afflictions outwardly are gain to us inwardly, if when the body is sick, and weak, and perishing, the soul is vigorous and prosperous. The best of men have need of further renewing of the inward man, even day by day. Where the good work is begun there is more work to be done, for carrying it forward. And as in wicked men things grow every day worse and worse, so in godly men they grow better and better. <div eID="gen31487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31488" type="x-p"/> 5. The prospect of eternal life and happiness kept them from fainting, and was a mighty support and comfort. As to this observe, (1.) The apostle and his fellow-sufferers saw their afflictions working towards heaven, and that they would end at last (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">v. 17</reference>), whereupon they weighed things aright in the balance of the sanctuary; they did as it were put the heavenly glory in one scale and their earthly sufferings in the other; and, pondering things in their thoughts, they found afflictions to be light, and the glory of heaven to be <hi type="italic">a far more exceeding weight.</hi> That which sense was ready to pronounce heavy and long, grievous and tedious, faith perceived to be light and short, and but for a moment. On the other hand, the worth and weight of the crown of glory, as they are exceedingly great in themselves, so they are esteemed to be by the believing soul—far exceeding all his expressions and thoughts; and it will be a special support in our sufferings when we can perceive them appointed as the way and preparing us for the enjoyment of the future glory. (2.) Their faith enabled them to make this right judgment of things: <hi type="italic">We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">v. 18</reference>. It is by faith that we see God, who is invisible (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">Heb. xi. 27</reference>), and by this we look to an unseen heaven and hell, and faith is the <hi type="italic">evidence of things not seen.</hi> Note, [1.] There are unseen things, as well as things that are seen. [2.] There is this vast difference between them: unseen things are eternal, seen things but temporal, or temporary only. [3.] By faith we not only discern these things, and the great difference between them, but by this also we take our aim at unseen things, and chiefly regard them, and make it our end and scope, not to escape present evils, and obtain present good, both of which are temporal and transitory, but to escape future evil and obtain future good things, which though unseen, are real, and certain, and eternal; and faith is <hi type="italic">the substance of things hoped for,</hi> as well as the evidence of things not seen, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.1">Heb. xi. 1</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Cor.4"/> <div eID="gen31488" type="x-p"/>

entries.df8afdf8a0c85901ee7881d1a69742670eaf5a47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17227"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen34207" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1-2Cor.4.18">2Co 4:1-18</reference>. His Preaching Is Open and Sincere, though to Many the Gospel Is Hidden.<div eID="gen34207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34208" type="x-p"/> For he preaches Christ, not himself: the human vessel is frail that God may have the glory; yet, though frail, faith and the hope of future glory sustain him amidst the decay of the outward man.<div eID="gen34208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34209" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17227"/><hi type="bold">1. Therefore--</hi>Greek, "For this cause": Because we have the liberty-giving Spirit of the Lord, and with unveiled face behold His glory (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.17">2Co 3:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen34209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34210" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeing we have this ministry--</hi>"The ministration of the Spirit" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">2Co 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.9">9</reference>): the ministry of such a spiritual, liberty-giving Gospel: resuming <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2Co 3:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.8">8</reference>.<div eID="gen34210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">received mercy--</hi>from God, in having had this ministry conferred on us (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>). The sense of "mercy" received from God, makes men active for God (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.11-1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:11-13</reference>).<div eID="gen34211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we faint not--</hi>in boldness of speech and action, and patience in suffering (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.16">8-16</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen34212" type="x-p"/>
entries.74269ca98f28fc8158d8c05ffa580ae198127e42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17228"/><div sID="gen34213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17228"/><hi type="bold">2. renounced--</hi>literally, "bid farewell to."<div eID="gen34213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of dishonesty--</hi>rather, "of shame." "I am not ashamed of the Gospel of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Ro 1:16</reference>). Shame would lead to hiding (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">2Co 4:3</reference>); whereas "we use great plainness of speech" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">2Co 3:12</reference>); "by manifestation of the truth." Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">2Co 3:3</reference>, "manifestly declared." He refers to the disingenuous artifices of "many" teachers at Corinth (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13-2Cor.11.15">11:13-15</reference>).<div eID="gen34214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">handling ... deceitfully--</hi>so "corrupt" or adulterate "the word of God" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.3">1Th 2:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen34215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commending--</hi>recommending ourselves: recurring to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>.<div eID="gen34216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to--</hi>to the verdict of.<div eID="gen34217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every man's conscience--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.11">2Co 5:11</reference>). Not to men's carnal judgment, as those alluded to (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.1">2Co 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen34218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the sight of God--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.17">2Co 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.1.10">Ga 1:10</reference>). <div eID="gen34219" type="x-p"/>
entries.a9ada1793aa293e3a6956985052fce0598422729: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17229"/><div sID="gen34220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17229"/><hi type="bold">3. But if--</hi>Yea, even if (as I grant is the case).<div eID="gen34220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hid--</hi>rather (in reference to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13-2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:13-18</reference>), "veiled." "Hid" (Greek, <reference osisRef="Col.3.3">Col 3:3</reference>) is said of that withdrawn from view altogether. "Veiled," of a thing within reach of the eye, but covered over so as not to be seen. So it was in the case of Moses' face.<div eID="gen34221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to them--</hi>in the case only of them: for in itself the Gospel is quite plain.<div eID="gen34222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that are lost--</hi>rather, "that are perishing" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">1Co 1:18</reference>). So the same cloud that was "light" to the people of God, was "darkness" to the Egyptian foes of God (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.20">Ex 14:20</reference>). <div eID="gen34223" type="x-p"/>
entries.93f13ab5723b7ee624642f602bff0fe26a3f22e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17230"/><div sID="gen34224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17230"/><hi type="bold">4. In whom--</hi>Translate, "In whose case."<div eID="gen34224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">god of this world--</hi>The worldly make him their God (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). He is, in fact, "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that ruleth in the children of disobedience" (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.2">Ep 2:2</reference>).<div eID="gen34225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minds--</hi>"understandings": "mental perceptions," as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>.<div eID="gen34226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them which believe not--</hi>the same as "them that are lost" (or "are perishing"). Compare <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.10-2Thess.2.12">2Th 2:10-12</reference>. South quaintly says, "when the malefactor's eyes are covered, he is not far from his execution" (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.8">Es 7:8</reference>). Those perishing unbelievers are not merely veiled, but blinded (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.15">15</reference>): Greek, not "blinded," but "hardened."<div eID="gen34227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34228" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">light of the glorious gospel of Christ--</hi>Translate, "The illumination (enlightening: the propagation from those already enlightened, to others of the light) of the Gospel of the glory of Christ." "The glory of Christ" is not a mere quality (as "glorious" would express) of the Gospel; it is its very essence and subject matter.<div eID="gen34228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34229" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">image of God--</hi>implying identity of nature and essence (<reference osisRef="John.1.18">Joh 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.15">Col 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). He who desires to see "the glory of God," may see it "in the face of Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2Co 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.14-1Tim.6.16">1Ti 6:14-16</reference>). Paul here recurs to <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>. Christ is "the image of God," into which "same image" we, looking on it in the mirror of the Gospel, are changed by the Spirit; but this image is not visible to those blinded by Satan [Alford]. <div eID="gen34229" type="x-p"/>
entries.abaa28453b1e231b19b631e03acd0645354e3185: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17231"/><div sID="gen34230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17231"/><hi type="bold">5. For--</hi>Their blindness is not our fault, as if we had self-seeking aims in our preaching.<div eID="gen34230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">preach ... Christ ... the Lord--</hi>rather, "Christ as Lord," and ourselves as your servants, &c. "Lord," or "Master," is the correlative term to "servants." <div eID="gen34231" type="x-p"/>
entries.479441ea79ee4e3a36a2e09c3989e46035d16216: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17232"/><div sID="gen34232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17232"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>proof that we are true servants of Jesus unto you.<div eID="gen34232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded the light--</hi>Greek, "By speaking the word, commanded light" (<reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Ge 1:3</reference>).<div eID="gen34233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath shined--</hi>rather, as Greek, "is He who shined." (It is God) who commanded light, &c., that shined, &c., (<reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference>): Himself our Light and Sun, as well as the Creator of light (Mal 4:2; <reference osisRef="John.8.12">Joh 8:12</reference>). The physical world answers to the spiritual.<div eID="gen34234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in our hearts--</hi>in themselves dark.<div eID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to give the light--</hi>that is, to propagate to others the light, &c., which is in us (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the glory of God--</hi>answering to "the glory of Christ" (see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Co 4:4</reference>).<div eID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the face of Jesus Christ--</hi>Some of the oldest manuscripts retain "Jesus." Others omit it. Christ is the manifestation of the glory of God, as His image (<reference osisRef="John.14.9">Joh 14:9</reference>). The allusion is still to the brightness on Moses' "face." The only true and full manifestation of God's brightness and glory is "in the face of Jesus" (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). <div eID="gen34238" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6364907296e73846ec3813f218ef0382b3d8e22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17233"/><div sID="gen34239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17233"/>7. "Lest any should say, How then is it that we continue to enjoy such unspeakable glory in a mortal body? Paul replies, this very fact is one of the most marvellous proofs of God's power, that an earthen vessel could bear such splendor and keep such a treasure" [Chrysostom, Homilies, 8.496, A]. The treasure or "the light of the knowledge of the glory of God." The fragile "earthen vessel" is the body, the "outward man" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16">2Co 4:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>), liable to afflictions and death. So the light in Gideon's pitchers, the type (Jud 7:16-20, 22). The ancients often kept their treasures in jars or vessels of earthenware. "There are earthen vessels which yet may be clean; whereas a golden vessel may be filthy" [Bengel].<div eID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the excellency of the power, &c.--</hi>that the power of the ministry (the Holy Spirit), in respect to its surpassing "excellency," exhibited in winning souls (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.4">1Co 2:4</reference>) and in sustaining us ministers, might be ascribed solely to God, we being weak as earthen vessels. God often allows the vessel to be chipped and broken, that the excellency of the treasure contained, and of the power which that treasure has, may be all His (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.30">Joh 3:30</reference>).<div eID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may be of God ... not of us--</hi>rather, as Greek, "may be God's (may be seen and be thankfully [2Co 4:15] acknowledged to belong to God), and not (to come) from us." The power not merely comes from God, but belongs to Him continually, and is to be ascribed to him. <div eID="gen34241" type="x-p"/>
entries.77a6408f945d0ba2d9da2ae573e5d73dae009a2a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17234"/><div sID="gen34242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17234"/>8. Greek, "BEING hard pressed, yet not inextricably straitened; reduced to inextricable straits" (nominative to "we have," <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>).<div eID="gen34242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">on every side--</hi>Greek, "in every respect" (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>, "always"; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>). This verse expresses inward distresses; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">2Co 4:9</reference>, outward distresses (<reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>). "Without were fightings; within were fears." The first clause in each member of the series of contrasted participles, implies the earthiness of the vessels; the second clause, the excellency of the power.<div eID="gen34243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perplexed, but not in despair--</hi>Greek, "not utterly perplexed." As perplexity refers to the future, so "troubled" or "hard pressed" refers to the present. <div eID="gen34244" type="x-p"/>
entries.68f6b6c6b6e233f12a753305c6ea47529a224403: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17235"/><div sID="gen34245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17235"/><hi type="bold">9. not forsaken--</hi>by God and man. Jesus was forsaken by both; so much do His sufferings exceed those of His people (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.46">Mt 27:46</reference>).<div eID="gen34245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast down--</hi>or "struck down"; not only "persecuted," that is, chased as a deer or bird (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.20">1Sa 26:20</reference>), but actually struck down as with a dart in the chase (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.35-Heb.11.38">He 11:35-38</reference>). The Greek "always" in this verse means, "throughout the whole time"; in <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference> the Greek is different, and means, "at every time," "in every case when the occasion occurs." <div eID="gen34246" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ace5b864516a3e38d72aba56c43eed5d5cbd5c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17236"/><div sID="gen34247" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17236"/><hi type="bold">10. bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus--</hi>that is, having my body exposed to being put to death in the cause of Jesus (the oldest manuscripts omit "the Lord"), and having in it the marks of such sufferings, I thus bear about wheresoever I go, an image of the suffering Saviour in my own person (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2Co 1:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.31">1Co 15:31</reference>). Doubtless, Paul was exposed to more dangers than are recorded in Acts (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.5">2Co 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.26">11:26</reference>). The Greek for "the dying" is literally, "the being made a corpse," such Paul regarded his body, yet a corpse which shares in the life-giving power of Christ's resurrection, as it has shared in His dying and death.<div eID="gen34247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body--</hi>rather, "may be." The name "Jesus," by itself is often repeated here as Paul seems, amidst sufferings, peculiarly to have felt its sweetness. In <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference> the same words occur with the variation, "in our mortal flesh. The fact of a dying, corpse-like body being sustained amidst such trials, manifests that "the (resurrection) life also," as well as the dying, "of Jesus," exerts its power in us. I thus bear about in my own person an image of the risen and living, as well as of the suffering, Saviour. The "our" is added here to "body," though not in the beginning of the verse. "For the body is ours not so much in death, as in life" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen34248" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcf1d29b7585ac13a28a32b0724242af07c680c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17237"/><div sID="gen34249" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17237"/><hi type="bold">11. we which live--</hi>in the power of Christ's "life" manifested in us, in our whole man body as well as spirit (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.10">Ro 8:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.11">11</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">2Co 4:10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.15">2Co 5:15</reference>). Paul regards his preservation amidst so many exposures to "death," by which Stephen and James were cut off, as a standing miracle (<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.23">2Co 11:23</reference>).<div eID="gen34249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34250" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered unto--</hi>not by chance; by the ordering of Providence, who shows "the excellency of His power" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.7">2Co 4:7</reference>), in delivering unto DEATH His living saints, that He may manifest LIFE also in their dying flesh. "Flesh," the very element of decay (not merely their "body"), is by Him made to manifest life. <div eID="gen34250" type="x-p"/>
entries.eec95b38704da2626d429c2108f30ae1b657a51f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17238"/><div sID="gen34251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17238"/>12. The "death" of Christ manifested in the continual "perishing of our outward man" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16">2Co 4:16</reference>), works peculiarly in us, and is the means of working spiritual "life" in you. The life whereof we witness in our bodily dying, extends beyond ourselves, and is brought by our very dying to you. <div eID="gen34251" type="x-p"/>
entries.87ed85660918b68a30d2bfdf909b033e3d49e340: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17239"/><div sID="gen34252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17239"/>13. Translate as Greek, "BUT having," &c., that is, not withstanding the trials just mentioned, we having, &c.<div eID="gen34252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the same spirit of faith, according as it, &c.--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Rom.8.15">Ro 8:15</reference>, on the usage of "spirit of faith." The Holy Spirit acting on our spirit. Though "death worketh in us, and life in you" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">2Co 4:12</reference>), yet as we have the same spirit of faith as you, we therefore [believingly] look for the same immortal life as you [Estius], and speak as we believe. Alford not so well translates, "The same ... faith with that described in the Scriptures" (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference>). The balance of the sentence requires the parallelism to be this, "According to that which is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak," namely, without fear, amidst "afflictions" and "deaths" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Co 4:17</reference>). <div eID="gen34253" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f8d3039ba7f433109f68dd09eba2f57b732f623: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17240"/><div sID="gen34254" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17240"/><hi type="bold">14. Knowing--</hi>by faith (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2Co 5:1</reference>).<div eID="gen34254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34255" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall raise up us also--</hi>at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1Co 6:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen34255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34256" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by Jesus--</hi>The oldest manuscripts have "with Jesus."<div eID="gen34256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">present us--</hi>vividly picturing the scene before the eyes (Jude 24).<div eID="gen34257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34258" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.14">2Co 1:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.19">1Th 2:19</reference>, 20; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">3:13</reference>). <div eID="gen34258" type="x-p"/>
entries.96f4ee03c43fc4047188d071ad3f4aa7a29a9e97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17241"/><div sID="gen34259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17241"/><hi type="bold">15. For--</hi>Confirming his assertion "with you" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.14">2Co 4:14</reference>), and "life ... worketh in you" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">2Co 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen34259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34260" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all things--</hi>whether the afflictions and labors of us ministers (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:8-11</reference>), or your prosperity (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.12">2Co 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8-1Cor.4.13">4:8-13</reference>).<div eID="gen34260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for your sakes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.10">2Ti 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen34261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abundant grace, &c.--</hi>rather, "That grace (the grace which preserves us in trials and works life in you), being made the greater (multiplied), by means of the greater number (of its recipients), may cause the thanksgiving to abound to the glory of God." [Chrysostom] (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.11">2Co 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.11">9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.12">12</reference>). The Greek is susceptible also of this translation, "That grace, being made the greater (multiplied) on account of the thanksgiving of the greater number (for grace already received), may abound (abundantly redound) to," &c. Thus the Greek for "abound" has not to be taken in an active sense, but in its ordinary neuter sense, and so the other Greek words. Thanksgiving invites more abundant grace (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.19-2Chr.20.22">2Ch 20:19-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">50:23</reference>). <div eID="gen34262" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e96ba054bec241914b4906efa8c0fd93b7015ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17242"/><div sID="gen34263" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17242"/><hi type="bold">16. we faint not--</hi>notwithstanding our sufferings. Resuming <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">2Co 4:1</reference>.<div eID="gen34263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">outward man--</hi>the body, the flesh.<div eID="gen34264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">perish--</hi>"is wearing away"; "is wasted away" by afflictions.<div eID="gen34265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">inward man--</hi>our spiritual and true being, the "life" which even in our mortal bodies (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2Co 4:11</reference>) "manifests the life of Jesus."<div eID="gen34266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34267" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is renewed--</hi>"is being renewed," namely, with fresh "grace" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">2Co 4:15</reference>), and "faith" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2Co 4:13</reference>), and hope (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2Co 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.18">18</reference>). <div eID="gen34267" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7974c5b26cdd9537e0206d3ad08c54f293e6c3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17243"/><div sID="gen34268" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17243"/><hi type="bold">17. which is but for a moment--</hi>"Our PRESENT light (burden of) affliction" (so the Greek; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">Mt 11:30</reference>), [Alford]. Compare "now for a season ... in heaviness" (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.6">1Pe 1:6</reference>). The contrast, however, between this and the "ETERNAL weight of glory" requires, I think, the translation, "Which is but for the present passing moment." So Wahl. "The lightness of affliction" (he does not express "burden" after "light"; the Greek is "the light of affliction") contrasts beautifully with the "weight of the glory."<div eID="gen34268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">worketh--</hi>rather, "worketh out."<div eID="gen34269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a far more exceeding and--</hi>rather, "in a surpassing and still more surpassing manner" [Alford]; "more and more exceedingly" [Ellicott, Trench, and others]. Greek, "in excess and to excess." The glory exceeds beyond all measure the affliction. <div eID="gen34270" type="x-p"/>
entries.041f3c59770f48edd3b76d003ccefadabb2f45b4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17244"/><div sID="gen34271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17244"/><hi type="bold">18. look not at--</hi>as our aim.<div eID="gen34271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things ... seen--</hi>"earthly things" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>). We mind not the things seen, whether affliction or refreshment come, so as to be seduced by the latter, or deterred by the former [Chrysostom].<div eID="gen34272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">things ... not seen--</hi>not "the invisible things" of <reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Ro 1:20</reference>, but the things which, though not seen now, shall be so hereafter.<div eID="gen34273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temporal--</hi>rather, "for a time"; in contrast to eternal. English Version uses "temporal" for temporary. The Greek is rightly translated in the similar passage, "the pleasures of sin for a season." <chapter eID="2Cor.4"/>

entries.2660e16f47cdd950ab8fb63c5fa9a61bc09d45d7: <div eID="gen48886" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen48887" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48888" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48888" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48887" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen48889" type="x-p"/> St. Paul shows the integrity with which he had preached the Gospel of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">2Cor 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Cor 4:2</reference>. And that, if it was unprofitable to any who had heard it, it was because their unbelieving hearts were blinded, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.3">2Cor 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.4">2Cor 4:4</reference>. How he preached, and how he was qualified for the work, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.5-2Cor.4.7">2Cor 4:5-7</reference>. The troubles and difficulties he met with in his labors, and the hope and consolations by which he was supported, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.8-2Cor.4.15">2Cor 4:8-15</reference>. And the prospect he had of eternal blessedness, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.16-2Cor.4.18">2Cor 4:16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen48889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48890" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen48890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48891" type="x-p"/> Seeing we have this ministry - The Gospel, of which he gave that noble account which we read in the preceding chapter. <div eID="gen48891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48892" type="x-p"/> We faint not - We meet with many tribulations, but are supported in and through all by the grace of the Gospel. Instead of ουκ εκκακουμεν, we faint not, ουκ εγκακουμεν, we act not wickedly, is the reading of ADFG, and some others. Wakefield thinks it the genuine reading; it certainly makes a very good sense with what goes before and what follows. If we follow this reading the whole verse may be read thus: Wherefore, as we have obtained mercy, or been graciously intrusted, ηλεηθημην, with this ministry, we do not act wickedly, but have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, etc.
entries.6b8bbc3ee876dcd145bdf1ef38d3a183d4995d83: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen48892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48893" type="x-p"/> But have renounced - Απειπαμεθα· We have disclaimed the hidden things of dishonesty; τα κρυπτα της αισχυνης, the hidden things of shame; those things which wicked men do; and which they are ashamed to have known, and ashamed to own. Dr. Whitby thinks that the apostle refers to carnal abominations, of which the Jews and their rabbins were notoriously guilty. And it does appear from the first epistle that there were persons in Corinth who taught that fornication was no sin; and it appears also that several had taken the part of the incestuous person. <div eID="gen48893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48894" type="x-p"/> Not walking in craftiness - Πανουργιᾳ· In subtlety and clever cunning, as the false teachers did, who were accomplished fellows, and capable of any thing. The word is compounded of παν, all, and εργον, work. <div eID="gen48894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48895" type="x-p"/> Nor handling the word of God deceitfully - Not using the doctrines of the Gospel to serve any secular or carnal purpose; not explaining away their force so as to palliate or excuse sin; not generalizing its precepts so as to excuse many in particular circumstances from obedience, especially in that which most crossed their inclinations. There were deceitful handlers of this kind in Corinth, and there are many of them still in the garb of Christian ministers; persons who disguise that part of their creed which, though they believe it is of God, would make them unpopular, affecting moderation in order to procure a larger audience and more extensive support; not attacking prevalent and popular vices; calling dissipation of mind, relaxation; and worldly and carnal pleasures, innocent amusements, etc. In a word, turning with the tide, and shifting with the wind of popular opinion, prejudice, fashion, etc. <div eID="gen48895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48896" type="x-p"/> But by manifestation of the truth - An open, explicit acknowledgment of what we know to be the truth - what we are assured is the Gospel of Jesus; concealing nothing; blunting the edge of no truth; explaining spiritual things, not in the words of man's wisdom, but in those taught by the Spirit of God. <div eID="gen48896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48897" type="x-p"/> Commending ourselves to every man's conscience - Speaking so that every man's conscience shall bear its testimony that we proclaim the truth of God. This is one characteristic of Divine truth: even every man's conscience will acknowledge it, though it speak decidedly against his own practices. <div eID="gen48897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48898" type="x-p"/> In the sight of God - Whose eye is ever on the heart and conscience of man, and who always bears testimony to his own word.
entries.da3fd94c51149f1af8872eb07928f6690d04801a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen48898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48899" type="x-p"/> But if our Gospel be hid - Κεκαλυμμενον· Veiled; he refers to the subject that he had treated so particularly in the conclusion of the preceding chapter. If there be a veil on the Gospel, it is only to the wilfully blind; and if any man's heart be veiled that hears this Gospel, it is a proof that he is among the lost, απολλυμενοι, those who are fully under the power of sin; who have given up themselves to work wickedness; persons who are mere heathens, or live like such, and yet such as Jesus Christ came to seek and save; for the word does not necessarily imply those that will perish eternally, but is a common epithet to point out a man without the Gospel and without God in the world. Christ commands his disciples in preaching the Gospel to go to προβατα τα απολωλοτα, the Lost sheep of the house of Israel; <reference osisRef="Mat.10.6">Mat 10:6</reference>; for himself says, <reference osisRef="Mat.18.11">Mat 18:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Luk.19.10">Luk 19:10</reference> : The Son of man is come ζητησαι και σωσαι το απολωλος, to seek and to Save that which is Lost. And such persons he represents under the parable of the lost sheep; for to find το απολωλος, that which is Lost, the good shepherd leaves the ninety-and-nine in the wilderness, and goes in search of it; <reference osisRef="Mat.18.12">Mat 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.15.4">Luk 15:4</reference>. The word more properly signifies, in all those connections, and in the parallel passages, not those who Are Lost, but those who are perishing; and will perish, if not sought and saved.
entries.c171ac8da523f72877dc614b0988d1bbe8aaa051: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen48899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48900" type="x-p"/> In whom the god of this world, etc. - We see here that those whose minds are blinded, are they who believe not; and because they believe not, their minds continue in darkness, and are proper subjects for Satan to work on; and he deepens the darkness, and increases the hardness. But who is meant by the god of this world? It is generally answered, the same who is called the prince of this world, <reference osisRef="Joh.16.11">Joh 16:11</reference>. But the question recurs, who is the prince of this world? and the answer to both is, Satan. The reader will do well to consult the notes on <reference osisRef="Joh.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>, and the concluding observations on <reference osisRef="Joh.14.30">Joh 14:30</reference>. I must own I feel considerable reluctance to assign the epithet ὁ Θεος, The God, to Satan; and were there not a rooted prejudice in favor of the common opinion, the contrary might be well vindicated, viz. that by the God of this world the supreme Being is meant, who in his judgment gave over the minds of the unbelieving Jews to spiritual darkness, so that destruction came upon them to the uttermost. Satan, it is true, has said that the kingdoms of the world and their glory are his, and that he gives them to whomsoever he will; <reference osisRef="Mat.4.8">Mat 4:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.9">Mat 4:9</reference>. But has God ever said so? and are we to take this assertion of the boasting devil and father of lies for truth? Certainly not. We are not willing to attribute the blinding of men's minds to God, because we sometimes forget that he is the God of justice, and may in judgment remove mercies from those that abuse them; but this is repeatedly attributed to him in the Bible, and the expression before us is quite a parallel to the following, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Isa 6:9</reference> : Go and tell this people, Hear ye indeed, but understand not; and see ye indeed, but perceive not. Make the Heart of this People Fat, and Make their Ears Heavy, and Shut their Eyes; Lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, etc. And see the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.14">Mat 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.13.15">Mat 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.4.12">Mar 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.12.40">Joh 12:40</reference>; and particularly <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8-Rom.11.10">Rom 11:8-10</reference> : God Hath Given Them the Spirit of Slumber, Eyes that they Should not See, and Ears that they Should not Hear; let their Eyes be Darkened, etc. Now all this is spoken of the same people, in the same circumstances of wilful rebellion and obstinate unbelief; and the great God of heaven and earth is he who judicially blinds their eyes; makes their hearts fat, i.e. stupid; gives them the spirit of slumber: and bows down their back, etc. On these very grounds it is exceedingly likely that the apostle means the true God by the words the god of this world. <div eID="gen48900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48901" type="x-p"/> And as to the expression this world, αιωνος τουτου, we are not to imagine that it necessarily means wicked men, or a wicked age; for it is frequently used to express the whole mundane system, and all that is called time: Whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither εν τουτῳ τῳ αιωνι, in This World, nor in the world to come; <reference osisRef="Mat.12.32">Mat 12:32</reference>. In <reference osisRef="Luk.20.34">Luk 20:34</reference>, the children, υἱοι του αιωνος τουτου, of This World, mean simply mankind at large in their state of probation in this lower world, in opposition to their state in the world to come. The same meaning the word has in several other places, to which l need not refer; it simply implying the present state of things, governed by the Divine providence, in contradistinction from the eternal state: and it is very remarkable that, in <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.17">1Tim 1:17</reference>, God himself is called Βασιλευς των αιωνων, the King of the World; what we call King eternal; but here it evidently means him who governs both worlds, and rules in time and eternity. This character among the Asiatics is considered essential to God; and therefore in the very first surat of the Koran he is called Rubbi Alalameen, "the Lord of both worlds," an expression perfectly similar to that above. But it is needless to multiply examples; they exist in abundance. Some, and particularly the ancient fathers, have connected του αιωνος τουτου with των απιστων, and have read the verse: But God hath blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world, etc. Irenaeus, Tertullian, Chrysostom, Theodoret, Photius, Theophylact, and Augustine, all plead for the above meaning; and St. Augustine says that it was the opinion of almost all the ancients. <div eID="gen48901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48902" type="x-p"/> Lest the light of the glorious Gospel - They have resisted the grace which God gave them, and have refused to yield to the evidences which amply prove the Messiahship of Jesus; and therefore their eyes were judicially darkened, as it is said in the prophet: He hath closed their eyes, and hath given them the spirit of slumber. That is, they have shut their eyes against the light, and their blindness and stupor are the consequence. <div eID="gen48902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48903" type="x-p"/> By glorious Gospel we are to understand the luminous Gospel; that which comes with so much light and evidence to every candid mind. <div eID="gen48903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48904" type="x-p"/> Who is the image of God - Christ is called, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb 1:3</reference>, the brightness of God's glory, and the express image of his person. See the note at <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">Heb 1:3</reference>.
entries.0e59f0284adad9b632ebe67c6cf65064d08200eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen48904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48905" type="x-p"/> For we preach not ourselves - We neither proclaim our own wisdom nor power; we have nothing but what we have received; we do not wish to establish our own authority, nor to procure our own emolument. <div eID="gen48905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48906" type="x-p"/> But Christ Jesus the Lord - We proclaim the author of this glorious Gospel as Christ, ὁ Χριστος, the same as המשיח hammashiach, the Messiah, the Anointed One; him of whom the prophets wrote; and who is the expectation, as he is the glory, of Israel, We proclaim him as Jesus יהושע Yehoshua, the Savior and Deliverer, who saves men from their sins. See <reference osisRef="Mat.1.21">Mat 1:21</reference>. And we proclaim Jesus of Nazareth to be the long-expected Messiah; and that there will be none other. And farther we proclaim this Jesus the Messiah to be the Lord, ὁ Κυριος, the great Ruler who has all power in heaven and earth; who made and governs the world; and who can save to the uttermost all that come to God through him. Such was the Redeemer preached by St. Paul. <div eID="gen48906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48907" type="x-p"/> And ourselves your servants - Labouring as fervently and as faithfully for your eternal interests as your most trusty slaves can do for your secular welfare. And we do this for Christ's sake; for although we by our labor show ourselves to be your servants, yea, your slaves, δουλους, yet it is a voluntary service; and we are neither employed by you nor receive our wages from you. We belong to Jesus; and are your servants on his account, and by his order.
entries.3f914e8db7b6d8977e3dc5f051641c030cfd5905: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen48907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48908" type="x-p"/> For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness - The apostle refers here to <reference osisRef="Gen.1.3">Gen 1:3</reference>. For when God created the heavens and the earth Darkness was on the face of the deep; and God said, Let There Be Light; and there was light. Thus he caused the light to shine out of darkness. <div eID="gen48908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48909" type="x-p"/> Hath shined in our hearts - He has given our hearts the glorious light of the Gospel, as he has given the world the glorious light of the sun. As sure, therefore, as God is the author of the light and the creator of the universe, so sure is he the author of the Gospel; it is no human invention; and is as far beyond the power of man's wisdom and might, as the creation of the world is beyond all created power, energy, and skill. <div eID="gen48909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48910" type="x-p"/> The light of the knowledge - To give us that light, that we might enlighten others; this appears to me to be the design of the apostle's προς φωτισμον της γνωσεως της δοξης του Θεου, or, as Dr. Whitby paraphrases it, to give us, and enable us to give to others, the light of the knowledge of God through Christ. <div eID="gen48910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48911" type="x-p"/> In the face of Jesus Christ - It is in and through Jesus that we can receive the Divine light, and it is in and by him that we can be made partakers of the Divine glory. The light mercy, holiness, and glory of God, are reflected upon and communicated to us through Jesus the Christ; and it is εν προσωπῳ, in the appearance and person of Jesus Christ that these blessings are communicated to us.
entries.02655f84a5722549a0450783d52a586ca5cb1b6b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen48911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48912" type="x-p"/> But we have this treasure in earthen vessels - The original, οστρακινοις σκευεσιν, signifies, more literally, vessels made of shells, which are very brittle; and as the shell is the outward part of a fish, it is very fit, as Dr. Hammond observes, to resemble our bodies in which our souls dwell. The Platonists make two bodies of a man: the one they call οξημα ψυχης, the chariot of the soul; the other, that which we see and touch; and this they call οστρακινον which is the same to us as the shell is to the fish. The word οστρακον not only signifies a shell, or vessel made of shell, but also πηλος ωπτημενος, an earthen vessel which has been burnt in the kiln, and earthen vessels or pottery in general; the difference between σκευη οστρακινα, earthen ware, and σκευη κεραμεως, the potter's vessel, is this: the latter implies the vessel as it comes out of the hands of the potter Before it is burnt; and the other is the vessel After it has passed through the kiln. St. Chrysostom, speaking of this difference, observes that the vessels once baked in the kiln, if broken, are incapable of being restored, δια την εκ τουπυρος εγγινομενην αυτοις ἁπαξ αντιτυπιαν, because of the hardness once gotten by fire; whereas the others are of clay unbaken, if they be spoiled ῥᾳδιωϚπρος το δευτερον επανελθῃ σχημα, they may easily, by the skill of the potter, be restored to some second form. See Hammond. This comports excellently with the idea of St. Paul: our bodies are in a recoverable form: they are very frail, and easily marred; but by the skill of the workman they may be easily built up anew, and made like unto his glorious body. The light and salvation of God in the soul of man is a heavenly treasure in a very mean casket. <div eID="gen48912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48913" type="x-p"/> The rabbins have a mode of speech very similar to this. "The daughter of the emperor thus addressed Rabbi Joshua, the son of Chananiah: O! how great is thy skill in the law, and yet how deformed thou art! what a great deal of wisdom is laid up in a sordid vessel! The rabbi answered, Tell me, I pray thee, of what are those vessels in which you keep your wines? She answered, They are earthen vessels. He replied, How is it, seeing ye are rich, that ye do not lay up your wine in silver vessels, for the common people lay up their wine in earthen vessels? She returned to her father, and persuaded him to have all the wine put into silver vessels; but the wine turned acid; and when the emperor heard it he inquired of his daughter who it was that had given her that advice? She told him that it was Rabbi Joshua. The rabbi told the whole story to the emperor, and added this sentence: The wisdom and study of the law cannot dwell in a comely man. Caesar objected, and said, There are comely persons who have made great progress in the study of the law. The rabbi answered, Had they not been so comely they would have made greater progress; for a man who is comely has not an humble mind, and therefore he soon forgets the whole law." See Schoettgen. There is a great deal of good sense in this allegory; and the most superficial reader may find it out. <div eID="gen48913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48914" type="x-p"/> That the excellency of the power may be of God; and not of us - God keeps us continually dependent upon himself; we have nothing but what we have received, and we receive every necessary supply just when it is necessary; and have nothing at our own command. The good therefore that is done is so evidently from the power of God, that none can pretend to share the glory with him.
entries.4fb05619fa7678fb36c9c462d63ff7fd696637ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen48914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48915" type="x-p"/> We are troubled on every side - We have already seen, in the notes on the ninth chapter of the preceding epistle, that St. Paul has made several allusions to those public games which were celebrated every fifth year at the Isthmus of Corinth; and those games have been in that place particularly described. In this and the three following verses the apostle makes allusion to the contests at those games; and the terms which he employs in these verses cannot be understood but in reference to those agonistical exercises to which he alludes. Dr. Hammond has explained the whole on this ground; and I shall here borrow his help. There are four pairs of expressions taken from the customs of the agones. <div eID="gen48915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48916" type="x-p"/> 1. Troubled on every side, yet not distressed. <div eID="gen48916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48917" type="x-p"/> 2. Perplexed, but not in despair. <div eID="gen48917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48918" type="x-p"/> 3. Persecuted, but not forsaken. Cast down, but not destroyed. <div eID="gen48918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48919" type="x-p"/> Three of these pairs belong to the customs of wrestling; the fourth, to that of running in the race. <div eID="gen48919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48920" type="x-p"/> Troubled on every side, etc. - Εν παντι θλιβομενοι. The word θλιβεσθαι, belongs clearly to παλη wrestling. So says Aristotle, Rhet. lib. i. cap. 5, (and the Scholiast on that place), ὁ γαρ δυναμενος - θλιβειν και κατεχειν, παλαιστικος· "He that can gripe his adversary, and take him up, is a good wrestler;" there being two dexterities in that exercise: <div eID="gen48920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48921" type="x-p"/> 1. to gripe, and <div eID="gen48921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48922" type="x-p"/> 2. to throw down, which Hesychius calls ωθειν and κρατειν; the first of these is here mentioned, and expressed by θλιβεσθαι, to be pressed down; to which is here opposed, as in a higher degree, στενοχωρεισθαι, to be brought to distress, as when one cannot get out of his antagonist's hands, nor make any resistance against him. So in Isaiah: στενοχωρουμενοι ου δυναμεθα μαχεσθαι, we are brought to such extremities that we can fight no longer. <div eID="gen48922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48923" type="x-p"/> Perplexed, but not in despair - Απορουμενοι, αλλ' ουκ εξαπορουμενοι. The word απορεισθαι, to be in perplexity, is fit for the wrestler, who being puzzled by his antagonist's skill knows not what to do: so in Hesychius, απορουντες, αμηχανουντες, they that are not able to do or attempt any thing, yet are not εξαπορουμενοι, they miscarry not finally, ορθοι ἱσταμενοι, stand after all upright; ουκ απογινωσκοντες και ἡττωμενοι, despair not, nor are they overcome, but find a happy issue out of all, being at last conquerors.
entries.3e79599abd342169acd10a501023673db9bdd06f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen48923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48924" type="x-p"/> Persecuted, but not forsaken - Διωκομενοι, αλλ' ουκ εγκαταλειπομενοι. The διωκομενοι, pursued, is peculiar to the δρομος, or race, when one being foremost others pursue, and get up close after him, endeavoring to outstrip him, but cannot succeed: this is the meaning of ουκ εγκαταλειπομενοι, not outstripped, or outgone, as the word implies. So in Plutarch: τους απολειφθεντας ου στεφανουσι, they do not crown them that are distanced or left behind. So says the apostle, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Cor 9:24</reference> : All run, but only One receiveth the Prize. <div eID="gen48924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48925" type="x-p"/> Cast down, but not destroyed - Καταβαλλομενοι αλλ' ουκ απολλυμενοι. This also belongs to wrestlers, where he that throws the other first is conqueror. And so Hesychius: καταβαλει, νικησει, ῥιψει, to cast down is to overcome, to throw. And then, the being not destroyed signifies that, although they were thrown down-cast into troubles and difficulties, yet they rose again, and surmounted them all.
entries.943d7d8d8c45c35c1db09efd92799af10dcc9411: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen48925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48926" type="x-p"/> Always bearing about in the body, etc. - Being every moment in danger of losing our lives in the cause of truth, as Jesus Christ was. We, in a word, bear his cross, and are ready to offer up our lives for him. There is probably an allusion here to the marks, wounds, and bruises which the contenders in those games got, and continued to carry throughout life. <div eID="gen48926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48927" type="x-p"/> That the life also of Jesus might be made manifest - That in our preservation, the success of our ministry, and the miracles we work, we might be able to give the fullest demonstration that Jesus is risen again from the dead; and that we are strengthened by him to do all these mighty works.
entries.6b9cd87373a7e41983bf0162728469a1759cdc0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen48927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48928" type="x-p"/> For we which live - And yet, although we are preserved alive, we are in such continual dangers that we carry our life in our hands, and are constantly in the spirit of sacrifice. But the life - the preserving power, of Christ is manifest in our continual support.
